title: Series Overview
text:
Series Policies

Attendance
We hope you will prioritize attendance of all classes in this series, but if you need to miss, please email the series instructor as early as possible. This will help us to share resources and plan for a smaller in-class community while you are out. Our hope is that you want to be present, but we totally understand that you have many demands on your time and sometimes life happens!
Please keep in mind that your presence in and contributions to class are important both to your understanding of the material and the creation and maintenance of our community of practice.


Usability, Accessibility, and Design
We are committed to creating a community of practice that is inclusive in its design. If you encounter barriers, please let the instructors know immediately so that we can determine if there is a design adjustment that can be made or if an accommodation might be needed to overcome the limitations of the design. We are always happy to consider creative solutions as long as they do not compromise the intent of the learning activity. We welcome feedback that will assist us in improving the usability and experience for all participants.

title: Planning for and Navigating Conflict
text:
In this session we will normalize conflict as a natural part of human interaction and adopt a proactive approach to preparing for it within our teams. We will explore typical modes of handling conflict, reflect on our individual and team patterns in approaching conflict, and identify supportive practices to ameliorate the challenges associated with over- or underuse of a particular conflict style.

title: Clear Communication, Courageous Conversations
text:
Most of us can name a conversation we have been putting off. A partner who keeps missing deadlines. A colleague whose comment in a meeting landed badly. A client whose expectations have quietly drifted from what we agreed to. We tell ourselves we are waiting for the right moment, but often we are waiting for the discomfort to go away. It rarely does, and in the meantime, the problem tends to grow. Having that conversation takes courage: stepping into uncertainty with openness, speaking honestly and with compassion, and listening deeply to the other person’s experience.
This session is designed to strengthen your communication skills and build capacity to engage in candid, sometimes difficult conversations about sensitive topics or conflicts with clarity, empathy, and effectiveness. We will explore the fundamentals of how we communicate and unpack why courageous conversations are valuable. We will share practical tips and approaches and apply them to real-world scenarios through guided practice. Building these skills supports confidence, authenticity, and stronger collaborative relationships.

title: Clear Communication, Courageous Conversations
text:
Why Courageous Conversations?
In the first session, we asked: What do I need, what do you need, and how do we agree to work together so everyone can do their best? Working agreements are a great start. But sooner or later, an agreement slips, a need goes unmet, or something lands badly. That’s when we need courageous conversations.
This session is organized around a single question:

How do I say what needs to be said, and hear what the other person needs me to hear, without making it harder than it has to be?

We will work on that question from the inside out:

The Ladder of Inference helps us notice what is happening in me: how quickly we move from what we saw to the story we are telling about it.
Nonviolent Communication gives us a way to say it clearly: to name what happened, how it affected us, what we need, and what we are asking for.
Listening for understanding helps us hear the other person: to find the needs underneath their words, which is often where common ground lives.


The Cost of Avoiding
Brené Brown popularized a simple phrase: “Clear is kind. Unclear is unkind.” It is tempting to believe that staying quiet, hinting, or softening a message until it disappears is the kind thing to do. Usually, it isn’t. When we avoid a hard conversation:

The other person loses the chance to understand the impact of their actions and to respond
We fill the silence with our own stories about what is going on, and those stories tend to get worse over time
Frustration leaks out sideways, in tone, in side conversations, or in withdrawal
Small, fixable problems become bigger, harder ones
Agreements stop meaning anything, because no one speaks up when agreements are broken

Courageous conversations are not about being blunt or winning an argument. They are about caring enough about the work and the relationship to say the true thing, with compassion. This is what we mean by candid communication: sharing truth while owning our impact on others, and when we are out of alignment, naming it and addressing it in real time. It is also an act of creative courage. Setting clear but kind boundaries is part of how we take care of ourselves, each other, and the work.






Note Pre-work (optional): Bring a Conversation to Mind





Before the session, think of a conversation you have been avoiding or one that you would like to handle better. It might be with a colleague, a client, or a partner in a collaborative. You won’t be asked to share the details. We will come back to it at the end of the session.
If you have a few extra minutes, skim the Feelings and Needs Inventory from the Center for Nonviolent Communication. We will use it later in the session.

title: Clear Communication, Courageous Conversations
text:
Fundamentals: Intent and Impact
Every message has two sides: what I meant (my intent) and how it landed (its impact). We judge ourselves by our intentions and others by their impact. When the two don’t match, each person tends to feel misunderstood: “That’s not what I meant!” and “But that’s how it came across!” are both true.
A few things widen the gap between intent and impact:

Channel. Text strips out tone of voice, facial expression, and timing. A short email that felt efficient to write can feel curt to read. The harder the message, the richer the channel it deserves (an in person conversation, call, or video rather than a chat message).
Power and position. The same words carry more weight coming from a supervisor, a funder, or a lead organization. Being aware of your position is part of communicating clearly.
Our own state. When we are tired, rushed, or anxious, a different part of us may be driving the bus, and our words come out differently than we intend.
Different thinking preferences. People listen for different things.


How Each Thinking Style Hears a Hard Message
Recall the Whole Brain Model from Session 1. When we are on the receiving end of a difficult conversation, our thinking preferences shape what we listen for and what helps us take it in.









Quadrant
Thinking style
Listens for
What helps




A - Blue
Analytical
What exactly happened?
Specific facts and examples, not generalizations


B - Green
Practical
What happens next?
A clear request and concrete next steps


C - Red
Relational
Are we okay?
Acknowledgement of the relationship and of feelings on both sides


D - Yellow
Experimental
Why does this matter?
The bigger picture and room to think about new options



Our natural tendency is to deliver hard messages in the way we would want to hear them. Thinking about the other person’s preferences can help you decide what to lead with, and what not to leave out. Adapting our language, tone, and style to the person in front of us is how candid communication connects effectively across differences.

title: Clear Communication, Courageous Conversations
section: Noticing Our Own Reactions: The Ladder of Inference
text:
Noticing Our Own Reactions: The Ladder of Inference
Before we can communicate clearly with someone else, it helps to notice what is going on inside ourselves. The Ladder of Inference, developed by organizational psychologist Chris Argyris and popularized by Peter Senge and colleagues in The Fifth Discipline Fieldbook, describes how quickly, and mostly unconsciously, we move from something we observe to a conclusion and an action.
Picture a ladder. At the bottom is everything that actually happened. Each step up takes us further from it:








Rung
What happens
Example




7. Actions
We act based on our beliefs
I stop including them in early planning conversations


6. Beliefs
We adopt beliefs about the world and this person
“I can’t count on them”


5. Conclusions
We draw conclusions
“They aren’t committed to this collaborative”


4. Assumptions
We make assumptions based on the meanings we added
“If they cared, they’d have told us sooner”


3. Meaning
We add meaning, based on our culture and experience
“A one-line reply means they don’t take this seriously”


2. Selected data
We notice some of it, and filter out the rest
I notice how short their message was


1. Observable data
What actually happened, as a camera would record it
They posted: “Our section will be late.”



Two things make the ladder especially tricky:

We climb it in seconds. It usually doesn’t feel like we’re making assumptions at all. It feels like we are just seeing what is obviously true.
It’s a loop. Our beliefs shape what data we notice next time. Once I believe someone is unreliable, I’m more likely to notice every late reply and less likely to notice when they come through. This is called the reflexive loop.

None of this means our conclusions are always wrong. It means they are worth checking before we act on them, especially when the stakes are high.

The Story I’m Telling Myself
Brené Brown offers a simple phrase that brings the ladder into a conversation: “The story I’m telling myself is…” Brown notes that our brains reward us for creating a story, even when it’s incomplete. Saying “the story I’m telling myself is that you aren’t committed to this, and I’d like to check that with you” names your conclusion as a story, not a fact. It shows the other person where you are on the ladder and invites them to help you climb back down. Saying this out loud is a small way to embrace vulnerability: you are owning where you are, admitting you might be wrong, and asking for the other person’s help to see more clearly.
This connects to the “parts” we explored in Session 1. When a part of us feels threatened (the Worrier, the Perfectionist, the part that hates being let down), it tends to climb the ladder fast. Noticing that you are high on the ladder is often a sign that a part has grabbed the wheel.






Warning Activity: Climbing Down the Ladder




Part 1 The scenarioPart 2 Climb up (individual)Part 3 Climb down (chat)


The scenario
You are six months into the multi-organization collaborative from Session 1. The group is preparing a joint funding proposal, and at the last monthly meeting each organization agreed to draft its section and post it in the shared folder by Friday. On Friday afternoon, Jamie, the representative from one partner organization, posts this in the group channel:

“Our section will be late. We have other priorities right now.”

Nothing else. The full draft is due to the funder in two weeks, and you are coordinating the proposal.


On your own (3 min), notice your first reactions. Jot down:

What story do you find yourself telling about Jamie or their organization?
What feelings come up?
What would you be tempted to do next?



In the chat (7 min), let’s climb back down together:

What is the observable data? What did Jamie actually say and do?
What other stories could explain the same data? Come up with as many as you can.
What don’t you know? What information would help you test your story?
What could you ask Jamie to find out?








Tool Highlight: Questions for Climbing Down the Ladder
Use these on your own, before a conversation, or whenever you notice a strong reaction:

What did I actually see or hear? What would a video camera have recorded?
What story am I telling myself about it? What else could be true?
What part of me is reacting? What is it trying to protect?
What data might I be filtering out?
What am I assuming about their intentions?
What could I ask to test my story?

And in conversation:

“Here’s what I noticed… and the story I’m telling myself is… Can you help me understand what’s going on?”
“What am I missing?”
“How do you see it?”

title: Clear Communication, Courageous Conversations
text:
Saying It Clearly: Nonviolent Communication
Once we have climbed down the ladder, we still need to say something. Nonviolent Communication (NVC), developed by psychologist Marshall Rosenberg, offers a simple structure for expressing ourselves honestly without blaming, and for hearing others without getting defensive. Rosenberg’s core insight is that behind every action, including the frustrating ones, is an attempt to meet a universal human need. When we connect at the level of needs, we can find more ways forward than when we argue about positions.
NVC has four components:








Component
What it is
Watch out for




Observation
What happened, described specifically and without evaluation
Mixing in judgment: “You’re always late,” “You ignored my email”


Feeling
How I feel about it, in words that describe my own internal state
“Faux feelings” that describe what someone did to me: ignored, disrespected, manipulated, abandoned


Need
The universal human need behind the feeling: clarity, reliability, respect, inclusion, rest
Confusing a need with a strategy: “I need you to reply within an hour” is a strategy; the need may be predictability


Request
A specific, doable action I’d like, framed as something the other person can say yes or no to
Demands, or vague requests like “be more responsible”




Naming What Happened: SBI + Intent
The observation is often the hardest part to get right, because our stories sneak into it. SBI + Intent gives it a shape:








Step
What it is
Example




Situation
When and where
“In Tuesday’s partner call…”


Behavior
What a camera would see or hear. No labels, no motives.
“…the timeline changed and our organization’s section moved up two weeks…”


Impact
What it did to me, including how I felt
“…and I felt caught off guard, because I’d already committed my staff’s time elsewhere.”


Intent
Theirs, not mine. Ask, don’t assume.
“Help me understand what was behind the change.”



Impact and intent are both true. A good intent doesn’t erase a hard impact, and a hard impact doesn’t prove a bad intent. Asking about intent is also a built-in way to climb down the ladder: you are checking your story instead of acting on it.


Asking for What You Need: The NVC Statement
Put together, NVC’s four components make a simple one-sentence form:

*“When ___ happens, I feel , because I need . Would you be willing to ___?“*

Notice that it says “because I need,” not “because you did.” In NVC, the other person’s action is what sparked the feeling, but the source of the feeling is your own need. That small shift keeps the statement about you rather than a verdict on them.
Two tips go with it:

State the emotion. No one can argue with how you felt. “I felt anxious” opens a conversation, while “you were careless” starts an argument.
Every ask gets a give. After you share what you need, invite the other person to share what they need: “What do you need from me?” It’s a trade, not a verdict. This is where common ground starts to show up.

You don’t need to use this structure word for word. In real conversations, it can sound stilted. The value is in the underlying moves: separating what happened from your interpretation, owning your feelings, naming the need, and making a clear request. For example:

Before: “You obviously don’t care about the proposal.”
After: “When I saw the message that your section would be late, without a new date, I felt anxious, because I need to be able to plan the full draft with the team and the funder deadline is close. Would you be willing to set up a quick call this week so we can figure out a timeline together?”



Needs Are Where Common Ground Lives
The most useful part of NVC for collaborative work may be the difference between needs and strategies. People rarely disagree about needs. Nearly everyone wants respect, fairness, reliability, being heard, and the chance to contribute. We disagree about strategies: the specific ways we try to meet those needs.
When a conversation feels stuck on positions (“We need the draft Friday” vs. “We can’t get to it until next month”), try asking what need each position is trying to meet. Often, there are several strategies that would meet both people’s needs, and finding them is far easier once the needs are on the table.
This is the same question we asked about working agreements in Session 1: What need does this serve, and whose need is it?






Warning Activity: Translate It




Part 1 TranslatePart 2 Possible translations


In the chat (8 min), pick one or two of these statements and rewrite them as an observation, a feeling, a need, and a request. Use the Feelings and Needs Inventory if it helps.

“You never read the materials before our meetings.”
“I feel like you’re ignoring my input.”
“This collaborative is completely disorganized.”
“You can’t just make that decision without us.”



There’s no single right answer. Here are some possibilities:

“In the last two meetings, a few questions came up that were answered in the pre-read (observation). I felt frustrated (feeling), because I want to use our meeting time well (need). Would you be willing to let me know if the pre-read isn’t arriving early enough for you to get to it (request)?”
“When I shared my idea in the meeting and we moved on without discussing it (observation), I felt discouraged (feeling), because I want my contributions to be considered (need). Would you be willing to come back to it at our next meeting (request)?” Notice that “ignored” is a faux feeling: it describes what you think someone did, not how you feel.
“We’ve rescheduled our last three meetings, and I wasn’t sure who was sending the agenda (observation). I feel uneasy (feeling) because I need some predictability to plan my time (need). Could we take ten minutes at the next meeting to agree on roles (request)?”
“I learned about the change in the workplan from the newsletter (observation). I felt surprised and a bit hurt (feeling), because I value being included in decisions that affect my organization (need). Can we talk about how decisions like this will be made going forward (request)?”

title: Clear Communication, Courageous Conversations
text:
Listening for Understanding
Speaking clearly is half of a courageous conversation. The other half, often the harder half, is listening. Most of us listen in order to reply: we are building our response while the other person is still talking. Listening for understanding means our goal, for now, is simply to understand what the other person is experiencing and what matters to them.
Listening for understanding is not agreeing. You can fully understand someone’s perspective and still disagree with it. But people are far more able to hear us once they feel heard.
Two of our core competencies live here. Active listening means staying fully present, asking open-ended questions, and building on others’ ideas while centering voices that are often unheard. To empathize is to listen deeply to others’ experiences, actively seek insight from their perspective, and connect with people from a place of love, respect, and curiosity.
A few practices help:

Get curious, not furious. Treat what you hear as information about the other person’s experience, not as an attack you need to defend against.
Reflect back what you heard, before you reply. Say it in your own words: “It sounds like the timeline has been really hard to manage alongside your other work. Did I get that right?” If they say no, try again until they say yes. It slows things down and means you are responding to what was actually said.
Listen for feelings and needs. In NVC terms, try to hear the feeling and need behind the words, especially behind blame or criticism. Someone who says “this process is a mess” may need clarity, or to feel that their time is respected.
Ask open-ended questions, not leading ones, and then actually listen to the answer. “What happened from your side?” invites the other person in. “Don’t you think that was a problem?” steers them toward your conclusion.
Embrace the silent space. After you ask a question or reflect something back, wait. People often share the most important thing after a pause.
Hold off on fixing. Advice, reassurance, and problem solving can all wait until the other person feels understood.
Notice your own ladder. If you find yourself getting defensive, that’s a cue that you have climbed up a rung or two. Pause, breathe, and come back to curiosity.


Tool Highlight: Curiosity Question Stems

“Help me understand…”
“What’s been going on for you with…?”
“What matters most to you about…?”
“What would a good outcome look like for you?”
“What’s getting in the way?”
“What am I missing?”
“Is there more?”

And for reflecting back:

“So what I’m hearing is… Did I get that right?”
“It sounds like you’re feeling ___ because ___ matters to you. Is that close?”







Warning Activity: Listening Pairs




Part 1 In pairsPart 2 Whole-Class Discussion


In pairs (12 min total)
The speaker talks for 3 minutes about a work situation that is mildly frustrating right now. Keep it low-stakes: a process that isn’t working, a tool you’re fighting with, a schedule that’s too full.
The listener may only:

Reflect back what they hear, including feelings and needs they notice
Ask open-ended questions (not leading ones)
Let silence happen. If the speaker pauses, wait before jumping in.

The listener may not give advice, share their own similar story, or reassure.
Then take 2 minutes to debrief:

Speaker: What did it feel like to be listened to this way?
Listener: What was hard about not fixing or relating?

Switch roles and repeat. The person whose first name comes first alphabetically speaks first.



What did you notice as the speaker? As the listener?
What urges did you have to resist as the listener?

title: Clear Communication, Courageous Conversations
text:
Practice: A Courageous Conversation
Now let’s bring all three tools together: noticing your own reactions, saying it clearly, and listening for understanding. We’ll start with Jamie’s scenario, then you’ll have a chance to prepare for a real conversation of your own.

Before the Conversation: Am I Ready?
A courageous conversation is more likely to go well when we go in prepared, not just with what we want to say, but with the right mindset. Brené Brown’s Engaged Feedback Checklist is a set of statements to check yourself against before giving feedback. Each one completes the sentence “I know that I’m ready to give feedback when…” Her central image is sitting next to the other person rather than across from them, with the problem in front of you both rather than between you. Her checklist also asks whether you are ready to listen and accept you may not fully understand, to own your part, to recognize the other person’s strengths, and to stay aware of power dynamics and bias.
If you can’t yet check most of the boxes, that’s useful information. It may mean you need more time on the ladder first. Or it may be a moment to embrace vulnerability and seek support: talking it through with a trusted colleague before the real conversation is a sign of strength, not weakness.


What It Sounds Like
Here is an example of what the full chain sounds like:

Speaker: “When the agenda changed an hour before the meeting, I didn’t have time to prepare the piece I was supposed to bring. I felt caught off guard, because I count on having time to get ready. What I need from you is a heads-up, even a quick one, before a change like that. And I’d like to understand what was going on for you.”
Listener (reflects first): “What I’m hearing is the timing made it hard to show up the way you wanted. Did I get that right?”
Listener (then shares their own needs): “That makes sense. From my side, when something comes up last minute, I feel pressure to get it on the agenda fast, because I don’t want to lose the window. What I need from you is some flexibility on short notice when it’s truly urgent.”

Name it concretely, reflect before responding, and trade asks rather than settling who’s right.






Warning Activity: Practicing the Conversation




Part 1 Triad PracticePart 2 Jamie’s rolePart 3 Whole-Class Discussion


The scenario continues
You’ve climbed down the ladder, and you’ve asked Jamie for a short call. You want to understand what’s going on, share the impact of the delay, and figure out a path forward together.
In groups of 3 (20 minutes)
Each person takes one role. The person whose first name comes first alphabetically plays the coordinator. The next plays Jamie. The third is the observer.

Coordinator: Open the conversation with SBI + Intent and an NVC statement. Then listen for understanding, and ask Jamie what they need from you.
Jamie: Read the “Jamie’s role” tab (others, please don’t peek!). Respond as Jamie would.
Observer: Keep time and take notes. Listen for: observations vs. evaluations, feelings and needs, reflecting back, curious questions, and moments where either person climbs up the ladder.


Prepare (3 min). The coordinator jots down an opening. Jamie reads their role. The observer reviews what to listen for.
Conversation (7 min). The coordinator and Jamie talk. Aim for understanding and a next step, not a perfect resolution.
Debrief (6 min). Jamie shares first: what helped you feel heard? What made you defensive? Then the coordinator, then the observer.
Capture (4 min). As a group, note one or two things that worked well to share with the whole group.



For the person playing Jamie only.
You care about this collaborative and believe in the proposal. Two weeks ago, your executive director told you that your organization’s board hasn’t yet decided whether it can commit staff time to the work the proposal would fund. Until the board decides in three weeks, you’ve been asked not to put anything in writing that commits your organization. You were embarrassed and unsure how much you were allowed to say, so you posted a short message and hoped to sort it out later.
You also feel a bit sidelined: at the last meeting, your suggestion about the proposal’s community engagement approach was set aside quickly, and you’re not sure your organization’s perspective is valued.
Start out a little guarded. If the coordinator is curious and doesn’t blame you, gradually share more. If you feel judged, keep it short.



What did the coordinator do that helped Jamie open up?
Where did people climb up the ladder? What brought them back down?
What needs did you discover underneath the positions? Where was the common ground?








Tool Highlight: Conversation Prep
Use this to prepare for a real conversation. You can work through it on your own or with a trusted colleague.
1. Check the ladder

What actually happened? What would a camera have recorded?
What story am I telling myself? What else could be true?
What part of me is reacting, and what is it trying to protect?

2. Get clear on my side

What am I feeling?
What do I need? (Not the strategy, but the need underneath it.)
What is my purpose for this conversation? What would a good outcome look like for both of us?
What is my part in this situation?

3. Consider their side

What might they be feeling and needing?
What might they want me to understand?
What’s their thinking preference, and what will help them hear me?
What power dynamics are at play between us?
Whose voices or perspectives might be missing from how I’m seeing this?

4. Plan my opening

SBI + Intent: Situation, behavior, impact, and a curious question about their intent
NVC statement: “When ___ happens, I feel ___ , because I need ___ . Would you be willing to ___ ?”
The give: “What do you need from me?”

5. Check my readiness

Review the Engaged Feedback Checklist. Am I ready to sit next to them, with the problem in front of us?
When and where will I have this conversation? Is the channel right for what I need to say?







Warning Activity: Your Own Conversation




Part 1 Individual PreparationPart 2 Sharing (optional)


On your own (10 min), bring to mind the conversation you thought about before the session, or another one you’d like to have. It can be big or small, current or past, work or personal. It doesn’t have to be dramatic, and it doesn’t need to involve anyone on this call. Choosing a smaller or less charged example than the first one that comes to mind is a perfectly good choice.
Work through the Conversation Prep prompts above. You don’t need to complete every prompt. Focus on the ones that feel most useful, and make sure you leave with your own NVC statement.
This is private. You won’t be asked to share the details of your situation.


In the chat or out loud, share only what you are comfortable sharing. Passing is always fine. If you share, keep it in the shape of an NVC statement (what you need) rather than a detailed account of what someone else did:

Which prompt was most useful?
What, if anything, shifted in how you see the situation?

title: Clear Communication, Courageous Conversations
text:
Taking It Back
The point of this session is to equip you to have these conversations in your own work: with your internal teams, with partners or clients, and in the collaborative teams we facilitate. A few reminders:

Clear is kind. Avoiding a conversation usually isn’t kinder. It just postpones the hard part and lets it grow.
Check your ladder first. Before you speak, separate what happened from the story you’re telling about it.
Lead with curiosity. You probably don’t have the whole picture. Ask before you conclude.
Name needs, not just positions. Needs are where common ground lives.
Every ask gets a give. After you share what you need, ask what they need from you.
Listen until they feel heard. People can hear you more easily once they feel understood.
Mind the channel and the power. Hard conversations deserve a rich channel, and your position shapes how your words land.
It doesn’t have to be perfect. A clumsy, caring conversation is almost always better than none. Creative courage means embracing experimentation and the inevitable mistakes that come with trying something new. You can always come back and say, “I’d like to try that again.”







Warning Discussion: What Will You Try First?






Which of today’s tools do you want to try first?
What conversation are you more ready to have now than when you arrived?




In our next session, Navigating Conflict, we will move from single conversations to patterns: the different ways we and our teams tend to handle conflict, when each approach is useful, and how to work through disagreements that are about more than a single conversation.
And one more time, the question that ties it all together: How do I say what needs to be said, and hear what the other person needs me to hear, without making it harder than it has to be?

title: Understanding Your Team: Thinking and Working Styles, Working Agreements
text:
Much of the friction on teams comes not from bad intentions, but from expectations nobody ever said out loud. One person assumes a quick reply on email is part of the job, while another expects to answer at the end of the day. One wants an agenda a day ahead, and another is happiest improvising. Neither is wrong. They just have different needs and defaults, and no one has talked about them.
This session will unpack what makes you and your colleagues or collaborators tick and the implications for how your team works together. We’ll explore individual thinking preferences, work styles, and values to deepen understanding and empathy across your team. Participants will gain practice in co-developing working agreements to ensure an inclusive and supportive environment in which all team members can show up fully and do their best work.

title: Understanding Your Team: Thinking and Working Styles, Working Agreements
text:
Why Understand Your Team?
This session is organized around a single question:

What do I need, what do you need, and how do we agree to work together so everyone can do their best?

We will look at it through two lenses and then put them to work:

Thinking preferences help us understand how I like to work: what we reach for, expect, and enjoy when things are going well.
Our many parts help us understand what happens when it gets hard: how different parts of us can take over under pressure.
Working agreements are how a team plans for both.

We start with preferences because they are the easiest to talk about, and then go a layer deeper. You can borrow this sequence when you work with your own teams and clients: begin with what is low-risk and easy to discuss, then build toward what takes more trust.






Note Pre-work: Thinking Preferences Quiz





Before the session, take this short quiz to understand your own thinking preferences better. Note which quadrant(s) you score highest in.
No time for the quiz? Read the quadrant descriptions below and pick the one that sounds most like you.

title: Understanding Your Team: Thinking and Working Styles, Working Agreements
section: Thinking Preferences: The Whole Brain Model
text:
Thinking Preferences: The Whole Brain Model
People have different thinking preferences, and those preferences influence what we expect and enjoy in group processes. Ned Herrmann’s Whole Brain Model offers a simple, memorable way to talk about those differences.
Herrmann’s model uses the brain as a metaphor. The neocortex is associated with intellectual, cerebral thinking and the limbic system with instinctive, emotional thinking. The left hemisphere is associated with rational, analytical, systematic thinking, and the right hemisphere with intuitive, artistic thinking. Combining these gives four quadrants, each associated with a different thinking style. As with any model, treat it as a useful lens and not a literal map of the brain.



Ned Herrmann’s Whole Brain Model


What Each Thinking Style Expects and Enjoys










Quadrant
Thinking style
Tends to ask
Expects
Enjoys




A - Blue
Analytical
What?
Clear, concise information; well-articulated ideas; accuracy and certainty
A good debate; critical analysis; readings


B - Green
Practical
When?
Step-by-step unfolding; a detailed program; punctuality; an explanation of how
A structured approach; low risk; concrete examples


C - Red
Relational
Who?
Involvement with others; personal anecdotes; an experiential approach; feelings to be considered
The personal touch; group discussion; harmony


D - Yellow
Experimental
Why?
An overview; a conceptual framework; freedom to explore; analogies and metaphors; visuals
Initiative and imagination; connections to other approaches; newness and fun



Most of us identify with more than one quadrant. Together, they describe a complex self made up of our rational, theoretical self; our ordered, safekeeping self; our emotional, interpersonal self; and our imaginative, experimental self. Your highest-scoring quadrant is where you tend to start, but the others are still part of you.
Why does this matter for teams and collaboratives? Because each thinking style brings different strengths and expectations for teamwork. The analytical colleague who asks for the data, the practical colleague who wants a clear plan and timeline, the relational colleague who wants to check in first, and the experimental colleague who wants to explore the big picture are all contributing something. Conflict can arise when each assumes their way is simply how work is done.
For more on how thinking styles shape meeting design, see Designing Meetings for All Thinking Styles in the Effective Meetings module.






Warning Activity: Expect and Enjoy




Part 1 Share your likes and dislikesPart 2 Compare and contrastPart 3 Discussion


Pick one thinking style to focus on for this activity – the one you scored highest in (if you have a tie, just pick one).
In the shared EasyRetro board:

Go to the columns for your style
Brainstorm things that make for a good small group or team process for you, and things that frustrate you (likes and dislikes)
Answer based primarily on the thinking preference you chose



On your own:

Read over the other columns
Notice where people with different thinking styles may have contrasting preferences




What strikes you as you read the other columns?
Where do you see overlap, and where do you see a real difference in what people expect?

title: Understanding Your Team: Thinking and Working Styles, Working Agreements
text:
Our Many Parts
The Whole Brain Model gives us shared language for differences in how people work. But it describes our preferences, what we reach for when things are going well. But we aren’t always at our best. Sometimes you feel overwhelmed, stuck, or burnt out. When you are feeling that way it may seem like the problem exists outside of you - we take on too much work, other people aren’t pulling their weight, etc. - but the source of the overwhelm (and the solution) may actually live inside of you.
Internal Family Systems (IFS) is a model from psychology, developed by Richard Schwartz, that starts from a simple observation: all of us have multiple sub-parts. They have different needs, fears, and ways of responding, and they compete for control over how we show up at any given moment. As Natalie Rofthels writes, “Some parts help you manage your time, and other parts help you lose track of time entirely; some think analytically, and others work intuitively and non-linearly; some strive for individual excellence, and others prioritize collaboration with your colleagues; some feel competent and confident, and others criticize you and tell you you’re not enough.”
When we are feeling stuck, it’s often because some voices have gotten really loud or are locked in an internal conflict, pulling you in different directions. The trick is to notice and listen to the competing voices within you.



My multiple parts


A helpful way to picture this is an internal bus. You are on the bus, and so are all of your parts. At any given moment, one of them is in the driver’s seat, whether or not you are aware of it. The part that jumps in with solutions, the part that gets defensive, and the part that wants everyone to get along may each take a turn at the wheel. Even the same person can show up quite differently depending on what is going on.



Your internal bus


Three additional ideas make this lens especially useful for teams:

All of our parts have positive intentions. Each is trying to help or protect us in some way, and each carries hope and wisdom. The part that gets defensive in a feedback conversation, for instance, may be trying to protect us from feeling like we’ve failed.
We each have a wise inner Self. This Self can help integrate our many parts and facilitate a dialogue among them to move through inner conflict. Ideally this wise Self is in the driver seat most of the time. When the Self is in the driver seat, people describe a feeling of being “centered.”
Awareness creates choice. We cannot always control which part reaches for the wheel, but when we notice who is driving, we have more room to respond thoughtfully instead of simply reacting.

A note on how we use this: we are borrowing IFS as a reflection tool for self-awareness at work. This is not intended as a form of therapy, and nothing here requires you to share more than you want to.






Warning Activity: Who’s been driving your bus?”




Part 1 - Individual ReflectionPart 2 - Pair Discussion


On your own reflect silently on these questions:

Which part of me has been most active this week? Who’s been driving my bus recently?
What is that part trying to do for me? What is it afraid of or hoping for?



In pairs:

Share what you noticed either about yourself or about the metaphor of the internal bus. Share only what you are comfortable sharing.







Tool Highlight: Reflection Prompts for Your Parts
You can use these prompts on your own, in a journal, or in a conversation with a trusted colleague. They work best when you ask them with curiosity rather than judgment.

Which part of me has been most active this week? What was going on when it showed up?
What is that part trying to do for me? What is it afraid of or hoping for?
How does it tend to show up in meetings or in conversations with teammates?
What does it need to feel more settled?
What would I want my teammates to know or do to help the part of me that does my best work take the wheel?

title: Understanding Your Team: Thinking and Working Styles, Working Agreements
text:
Core Values
Our values are another way to understand what is driving us. They are the beliefs that are most important to you and that fill you with purpose. They should resonate deeply with how you identify as a person. You may already know what your core values are.
If you want to discover them, Brené Brown’s work offers a practical starting point:

Scan her list of values; feel free to add new values or put these in your own words.
Narrow it down to the two or three that are most central to you. You may want to start by circling 10-20 that resonate with you and then whittling down your list.
Your secondary values may be nested under your core values - your commitment to those values is likely fueled by your one to two core values (e.g., my commitment to collaboration is fueled by the value I place on learning and making a difference)

Once you have identified your core values, sharing them with team members or collaborators can be a powerful way to build understanding and empathy. And you can start to practice aligning your behavior more intentionally with your values. Explore the prompts below on your own to deepen your understanding of how your values shape how you show up.

Tool Highlight: Living into Your Core Values
You can use these prompts on your own, in a journal, or in a conversation with a trusted colleague or friend.

What does it feel like when you are living into your values?
What are early warning signs for you that you are out of integrity with your core values?
What are 3-4 behaviors that support you in living into each of your core values?
What are 3-4 slippery behaviors you find yourself tempted to engage in even though they are counter to your core values?
Who is someone who knows your values and supports your efforts to live into them? What does support from this person look like?
How does living into your values shape the way you give and receive feedback?
What can you do as an act of self compassion to support yourself in the hard work of living into your values?

Read back over what you wrote. Circle words or phrases that stand out to you. Identify a behavior that supports your core values that you want to focus on in the coming months.

title: Understanding Your Team: Thinking and Working Styles, Working Agreements
text:
You at Your Best
We now have three lenses: how we prefer to work, our core values, and what shows up under stress. This next step pulls them together around one question: what helps you do your best work?






Warning Activity: Guided Journaling




Part 1 - Individual Reflection- Part 2 - Sensemaking


Reflect on a work experience, at LegacyWorks or elsewhere, that felt satisfying, enlivening, and productive. It should be a time that reflects you at your best. Then jot down some notes in response to these questions:

What were you doing?
What were others doing?
What enabled that great work experience?
What helped you to be your best?
What do you really value?
What is most important to you when you think about how you want your work environment to feel, how you want to show up, and how you want to be treated?



Read back over what your wrote. Circle words or phrases that stand out to you. Distill your notes into two or three things you need to do your best work, and one or two things you offer a team.





You just named what you need. Now imagine everyone on a team did the same, and most of it was never said out loud. How does a team figure out what everyone needs, and then act in accordance with that?

title: Understanding Your Team: Thinking and Working Styles, Working Agreements
text:
Working Agreements
One way is through working agreements: statements of how we will show up with and for each other.
Why are they valuable? Working agreements:

Allow team members to communicate what is important to them and how they like to work
Help create the conditions for everyone to show up as the best version of themselves
Increase mutual accountability, because expectations are visible and shared


A Note on Terminology
You will hear working agreements called many things. The names overlap, and what matters more than the label is whether the team made them together and they do real work. That said, the terms carry slightly different connotations, so choose the one that best fits your team culture and context.








Term
Typical feel
Where it fits best




Working agreements
Practical and team-made: how we will work together day to day
Ongoing teams and project teams


Ground rules
Short, often set by a facilitator, for a particular meeting or session
One-off meetings, workshops, and convenings


Norms
Can describe how a group actually behaves as well as how it intends to
Groups reflecting on or reshaping their existing culture


Principles
Higher level and values-based, less behavioral
Guiding the overall approach of a collaborative, alongside agreements


Code of conduct
Formal, often organization-wide, tends to imply standards and consequences
Organizations, large communities, and events


Collaboration agreement
Partnership-flavored, can sound contract-like
Multi-organization collaboratives and client partnerships



Words like “rules” and “code of conduct” can sound imposed, while “agreement” signals shared ownership. When you work with a client or a larger collaborative, check what language feels comfortable to them. Or ask the group what they want to call it. How people respond is a quick test of whether they feel ownership.


Where Might We Need Them?
Working agreements are useful anywhere people work together over time, across the nested scales at which we work:

Internal teams - to set expectations for communication, meetings, availability, and decision making
Collaboratives and partnerships - where no one is in charge by default and agreements are part of setting the culture of the collaborative
Clients and consulting engagements - to understand and show up in the way your client expects and enjoys
Communities - to define how members engage with each other




LegacyWorks Group nested scales


You may even want to consider some commitments you want to make to yourself to help your best self show up in the workplace. Maybe you agree to speak your needs to the group, even when it causes you discomfort, or to get adequate sleep, exercise and nutrition to sustain your energy. What do you need that only you can provide?


Ingredients of a Good Agreement
Not all agreements are equally useful. “Communicate openly” and “respect each other’s time” sound good, but they don’t tell anyone what to do. Strong agreements tend to share five ingredients:







Ingredient
What it means




Specific and behavioral
Says who does what, by when, so you could tell whether it happened


Tied to a real need
Exists because it supports how people work best, not because it sounds good


Plans for exceptions
Says what happens when it can’t be followed or gets broken, and who decides


Co-created
Built with everyone who is expected to follow it, not handed down


Revisited
Includes a point to check whether it’s working and adjust



The first three of these ingredients live in the wording of the agreement. The others (co-created, revisited) speak to the process for creating and implementing the agreement. These might not be explicit in the language, but they make the difference between an agreement people follow and a poster on the wall.

Weak and Strong Examples









Context
Weak
Strong
What the strong version adds




Communication
“We’ll communicate openly.”
“If you’re blocked or going to miss a deadline, tell the team as soon as you know, not at the next check-in.”
Specific and behavioral: you could tell whether it happened


Meetings
“We’ll respect each other’s time.”
“Meetings start and end on time. Agendas go out 24 hours ahead, and we release the meeting time if there’s nothing for the agenda.”
Observable actions with a clear trigger; also serves people who need prep time


Responsiveness
“We’ll be responsive.”
“We respond to messages within one working day. For anything urgent, call or text. Otherwise, we won’t expect a same-day reply.”
Defines what “responsive” means and separates urgent from non-urgent


Decisions
“We’ll make decisions together.”
“For decisions that affect everyone, we gather input for a week, then the project lead decides and explains the reasoning. For small decisions, whoever owns the task decides.”
Clarifies how “together” works and who holds authority



Here is an example that includes all five ingredients:

“We keep Fridays free of internal meetings so people who need uninterrupted time can do deep work. If something urgent comes up, anyone can ask for an exception, and the team lead decides. If we notice this isn’t working, anyone can raise it at our next check-in, and we’ll revisit it.”

It is specific (no Friday meetings), tied to a need (protected focus time), has a plan for exceptions (how to ask, who decides), and has a review point (the regular check-in). It also only works if the team agreed to it together.


Sounds Good, but Is It Tied to a Need?
An agreement can be specific and still fail the test, because it is borrowed from a general idea of what good teams do or from one person’s preference, instead of coming from the people in the room.

“No emails after 6 pm.” Sounds like good work-life balance, but it solves a problem nobody has if the team spans time zones or some people prefer to clear their inbox in the evening. A need-based version might be: “Nothing sent after 6 pm requires a response before 10 am the next day,” which addresses the real concern of not feeling on call.
“Everyone keeps their camera on.” Sounds like it builds connection, but it adds friction for someone with a poor connection, a need to move around, or camera fatigue. The underlying need, feeling connected and knowing people are engaged, can be met in other ways.
“We’ll start every meeting with a check-in round.” Great for relational thinkers, but it may feel like a time-waster to someone who wants to get to the agenda. If no one on the team has expressed a need for it, it is a nice idea and not (yet) an agreement.

The question to ask is: What need does this serve, and whose need is it? An agreement that comes from one person’s need isn’t automatically wrong. “I need agendas ahead of time” can become a team agreement if others see the value or can easily accommodate it. The point isn’t that everyone shares the need. It is that the need is visible, so people can make a real choice instead of agreeing to something that sounds good.
Because agreements should be based on the needs of the actual humans trying to work together, they should be built by the team, for the team and revisited whenever team composition shifts. Some moments when it is especially worth having this conversation include:

At the start of a meeting you are facilitating for a new group or a group that comes together infrequently
At the beginning of a new year or new project
When team membership or leadership changes
When you begin working with a new client or partner




Starting the Conversation
Working agreements can be built through many kinds of conversations, from a quick check in at the start of a meeting to a more in depth team process. When working with a new client or partner, an initial intake conversation is a great way to elicit material for working agreements. We do this at the start of a relationship, not once friction appears, so that we can show up in the way our partners expect and enjoy. Below are some example questions you can use when establishing a new partnership or client relationship. And here’s an example agenda for an initial client launch meeting with some of these questions embedded – feel free to reuse and adapt!

Sample Questions
Communication

How do you prefer to communicate and what are your urgency levels for each channel, e.g. Slack DMs for general updates, texts for emergencies.
If someone on the team needs an immediate response, what’s the best way (email, text, phone call)?

Availability & Scheduling

When will you be available for the team? What are your standard working hours?
Do you have preferred times for one type of work over another, e.g. you want to write in the mornings and have meetings in the afternoons?
How much advance time do you need for scheduling calls or virtual meetings?

Approach to Collaboration

How do you prefer to collaborate? Do you like to confer then divide up tasks and work side by side? Be given specific tasks to complete and then report back? Work on the same task simultaneously (e.g. in a shared doc)?
What are your superpowers (strengths)? What are you great at and love?
What’s your kryptonite (weaknesses)? What stresses you out, and how can we navigate that stress?
What do you want help with or want to delegate?
A meeting / collaboration pet peeve is…
What suggestions do you have for making the best of our collaboration?

Reflection & Review

I think best by… (e.g. writing, having time to reflect, talking, drawing, moving…)
How much advance time do you need for reviewing things?
Do you prefer to iterate early drafts or see polished products?

Platforms and tools

What platforms and software tools do you use for sharing documents, communication, virtual meetings?
Are there any you cannot use due to institutional restrictions?



Matching Depth to Context
You don’t need to use every lens every time. Match the depth of the conversation to the relationship and the level of trust:







Situation
Approach




A new client or short-term collaboration
A light work style questionnaire: quick, practical, and low-vulnerability


An ongoing team with some trust
Thinking preferences, plus the “you at your best” reflection, to understand each other’s defaults and what matters


A team with real trust, or one working through friction
Add the parts reflection, which asks for more openness





What Agreements Can Be About
If you’re not sure where to start, here is a menu of topics that agreements commonly cover:

Equitable participation and inclusivity
Communication norms (e.g., openness, honesty, vulnerability)
Giving and receiving feedback
Communication channels and response times
Meetings (purpose, length, agendas, who attends)
Availability and working hours
Review and feedback (how much time, in what form)
Decision making authority and model (scope and who and how we make decisions)
How we handle disagreements, mistakes, and slipped agreements




Tool Highlight: Min Specs
Min Specs is a Liberating Structure well suited to developing working agreements, especially with experimental thinkers who may be wary of lots of rules. Individuals brainstorm the things the group must do or must not do to achieve its purpose, share in pairs or small groups, and then pare the list down to the minimum set of rules the group could follow and still achieve its purpose. It pairs naturally with 1-2-4-All for engaging everyone. For more on these and other microstructures, see the Effective Meetings module.


Practice: Co-developing Working Agreements
You’ve seen the ingredients and a real-world example. Now it is time to try it. Your drafts don’t need to be perfect. We are practicing the process.






Warning Activity: Drafting Working Agreements




Part 1 - Small Group DiscussionPart 2 - Whole-Class Discussion


The scenario
You’ve just joined a new collaborative made up of representatives from several organizations working toward a shared community goal. No single organization is in charge, and the group will work together for the next year, meeting virtually once a month. Members have very different amounts of time to give, and some can make decisions on the spot while others need to check with a board or supervisor first. At your first meeting, the group decides to draft working agreements before getting into the work.
In small groups of 3-4 (18 minutes)
You’ll play yourself, bringing your own working style and the needs and offers you jotted down in the journaling activity. Choose one person to record in the shared notes document.

Share (4 min). Going around the group, each person shares one need and one offer. The person whose first name comes first alphabetically starts.
Notice (3 min). Where do your needs overlap? Where do they differ?
Draft (8 min). Turn two or three of your needs into agreements for this collaborative. Two or three is plenty. Aim for agreements that someone could actually observe.
Check (3 min). Test each draft against the five ingredients. Revise anything that falls short.

You’re done when you have two or three draft agreements and have checked each against the ingredients. They don’t need to be perfect. We are practicing the process.
When we return, be ready to share one agreement and why you wrote it that way.


As a whole class, let’s discuss:

Which ingredients were easy to meet? Which were hard?
Whose needs showed up in your draft? Whose might have been left out?
What did you notice about the process, as someone who may run it?
What would you do differently with a real team?








Taking It Back
The point of this session is to equip you to use these tools in your own work: with your internal teams, with partners or clients, and in the collaborative teams we facilitate. A few reminders as you do:

Start with the “why.” People are more willing to engage when they understand what agreements are for and what’s in it for them.
Choose the right depth for the situation. A new client may only need a few quick work style questions. A longer-standing team may be ready for more.
Make the process as inclusive as the content. Use the same moves you would use in any good meeting: give people time to think before sharing, offer different ways to contribute, and invite quieter voices.
Name the need behind every agreement. If you can’t, it may be a candidate for dropping or revising.
Plan to revisit. Teams change, and so do needs.



Revisiting Agreements
Agreements aren’t set in stone. Build in regular check-ins, such as a standing agenda item once a quarter, or a trigger like a change in membership or leadership. Some simple prompts:

What’s working?
What’s not working, or not getting followed?
What’s changed since we wrote these?
Is anything missing?







Warning Discussion: What Will You Try First?






You’ll do this with your own teams and partners. What do you want to try first?
What do you need in order to start that conversation?




And one more time, the question that ties it all together: What do I need, what do you need, and how do we agree to work together so everyone can do their best?
